      "text": "We computed the character distributions of each language on our development set and defined an arbitrary accepted character set for each of them by considering all characters falling within the first 95th percentile."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q216",
      "page": 30,
      "dimension": "input_form",
      "text": "We consequently filtered out any sentence from our training set that was composed of less than 80% of such accepted characters."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q217",
      "page": 30,
      "dimension": "input_form",
      "text": "For languages whose script spans thousands of characters, the character histogram method mentioned above was not as effective since the character distribution trends were less prominent."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q218",
      "page": 30,
      "dimension": "output_content",
      "text": "As an alternative, linguists provided Unicode ranges to define accepted character sets."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q219",
      "page": 30,
      "dimension": "input_form",
      "text": "Any sentence containing less than 50% of characters from that set was eventually discarded."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q220",
      "page": 31,
      "dimension": "input_form",
      "text": "Linguists also pointed out that many mislabeled training samples were actually plain English sentences. This can be explained by the massive prevalence of English on the web, even on pages primarily written in other languages. We built a simple, dedicated binary fasttext classifier to filter these samples out of our training dataset."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q221",
      "page": 31,
      "dimension": "output_form",
      "text": "This section presents a comparison of our approach to existing publicly available models on both Flores-200 and annotated noisy web data, followed by an error analysis."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q222",
      "page": 31,
      "dimension": "output_form",
      "text": "We analyze the performance of our LID models on the Flores-200 dataset from Section 4 and compare to other open-source models. We utilize Flores-200 for evaluation as the target-side text is human-verified as being in the right language. Utilizing standard public datasets for evaluation is less reliable given they often contain untrustworthy language labels and are quite noisy (Kreutzer et al., 2022)."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q223",
      "page": 31,
      "dimension": "output_form",
      "text": "We compare our LID model with three publicly available models: CLD3, LangId and LangDetect. Table 4 reports performance of our final LID model on the set of various language intersections covered by all four models. Micro F1 scores and False Positive Rates across all languages found in Flores-200 are displayed in Table 5."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q224",
      "page": 31,
      "dimension": "output_form",
      "text": "Given the different scopes of languages supported, we report on 3 cascading intersections with Flores-200: (1) the 51 languages also supported by LangId, LangDetect and CLD3, (2) the 78 languages also supported by LangId and CLD3 and (3) the 95 languages also supported by CLD3. We report metrics of all models across all intersections to reflect the impact of false positives on unseen languages."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q225",
      "page": 31,
      "dimension": "output_form",
      "text": "Our model is capable of handling the 200 languages of Flores-200 (compared to the 107 languages supported by CLD3) while achieving significantly higher performance than all three of LangId, LangDetect and CLD3. Furthermore, the gain in F1 score is accompanied by a noticeable improvement in False Positive Rate, suggesting a much stronger fit for extracting low-resource languages from web corpora (Caswell et al., 2020)."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q226",
      "page": 31,
      "dimension": "input_content",
      "text": "Despite strong results on Flores-200, we expect a sizable gap in performance when applying our LID model to our target web data."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q227",
      "page": 32,
      "dimension": "input_content",
      "text": "Indeed, various sources of noise such as language mixing, creative use of various scripts, and leetspeak are widespread online."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q228",
      "page": 32,
      "dimension": "input_content",
      "text": "Extracting sentences from internet pages is also prone to unexpected artifacts introduced after parsing."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q229",
      "page": 32,
      "dimension": "output_form",
      "text": "There is no readily available evaluation set from the web domain on which to properly assess and tune performance, let alone iterate on design choices when modeling."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q230",
      "page": 32,
      "dimension": "input_content",
      "text": "To this end, we select 74 low-resource languages on which our preliminary LID model yield low F1 scores."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q231",
      "page": 32,
      "dimension": "input_content",
      "text": "After a first run of language identification on web data, we randomly selected several thousand sentences across various languages for which prediction scores fell between 50% and 90%."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q232",
      "page": 32,
      "dimension": "input_form",
      "text": "That hard threshold was chosen upon manual inspection, noticing that many classification errors were found within that range."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q233",
      "page": 32,
      "dimension": "output_content",
      "text": "Human annotators were tasked with inspecting our random sentences and assessing whether each was indeed in the predicted language."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q234",
      "page": 32,
      "dimension": "output_ontology",
      "text": "Based on these annotations, we built a challenge set for language identification to benchmark our final LID model."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q235",
      "page": 32,
      "dimension": "input_content",
      "text": "As shown on Table 6, we achieve lower performance than on the Flores-200 dataset, hinting at a non-negligible domain mismatch."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q236",
      "page": 32,
      "dimension": "output_form",
      "text": "As suggested in Caswell et al. (2020), we report False Positive Rates (FPR) on top of F1 scores, to get a better picture of how well our model would fare"
    },
    {
      "id": "Q237",
      "page": 33,
      "dimension": "output_content",
      "text": "It should be noted that since the sentences to annotate were chosen based on a previous model, this challenge set is biased by that underlying intermediate model."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q238",
      "page": 33,
      "dimension": "output_content",
      "text": "We worked closely with linguists to analyze them."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q239",
      "page": 33,
      "dimension": "input_ontology",
      "text": "Upon inspection, we found that these language pairs correspond to highly similar languages, displaying major vocabulary and grammar overlap."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q240",
      "page": 33,
      "dimension": "input_ontology",
      "text": "For example, Asante Twi (aka_Latn) and Akuapem Twi (twi_Latn) are two mutually intelligible languoids of the Akan language continuum, which share common words, phrases, or even identical sentence translations."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q241",
      "page": 33,
      "dimension": "output_content",
      "text": "This suggests that from a linguistic point of view, the LID confusion found in these similar languages is to be expected and is not a symptom of a deeper modeling issue."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q242",
      "page": 33,
      "dimension": "output_content",
      "text": "In practice, this means prediction performance might be underestimated for some languages and calls for collecting and accepting multiple language labels in future work."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q243",
      "page": 33,
      "dimension": "output_form",
      "text": "We noticed that predictions tend to be more robust for long sentences."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q244",
      "page": 33,
      "dimension": "output_form",
      "text": "This is consistent with an observation by Jauhiainen et al. (2017) and could be further investigated."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q245",
      "page": 33,
      "dimension": "output_form",
      "text": "A potential mitigation strategy would be to tune our models on a more balanced development set with respect to length."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q246",
      "page": 33,
      "dimension": "input_form",
      "text": "In our current approach, we mitigate this issue by applying length filters in the downstream monolingual pipeline described in Section 5.2."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q247",
      "page": 34,
      "dimension": "input_form",
      "text": "We synthetically create test samples of a specific length without cutting words, except for languages with continuous scripts."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q248",
      "page": 34,
      "dimension": "input_content",
      "text": "Monolingual data is a valuable resource which can be used for a variety of downstream tasks such as bitext mining, backtranslation, and language model training."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q249",
      "page": 34,
      "dimension": "input_content",
      "text": "Additionally, data quality can have a large impact on the performance of such tasks."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q250",
      "page": 34,
      "dimension": "input_content",
      "text": "In order to maximize the potential benefits of leveraging these data sources, we aim to produce high quality and clean monolingual data."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q251",
      "page": 34,
      "dimension": "input_content",
      "text": "As discussed earlier in this section, such data can be scarce, particularly in the low-resource setting."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q252",
      "page": 34,
      "dimension": "input_content",
      "text": "We therefore decided to extend the work done in CCNet, CCMatrix (Schwenk et al., 2021b; Wenzek et al., 2020), and others like OSCAR (Ortiz Suárez et al., 2019)."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q253",
      "page": 34,
      "dimension": "input_content",
      "text": "In this section, we describe our end-to-end process for both curating and cleaning monolingual data."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q254",
      "page": 34,
      "dimension": "input_content",
      "text": "We begin with web data as our starting point, provided by CommonCrawl (CC) and ParaCrawl (Bañón et al., 2020)."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q255",
      "page": 34,
      "dimension": "input_form",
      "text": "This data has been preprocessed to remove all markup and (approximately) normalize encoding to UTF-8."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q256",
      "page": 34,
      "dimension": "input_form",
      "text": "HTML stripping converts block tags to newlines while inline tags are removed."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q257",
      "page": 34,
      "dimension": "input_form",
      "text": "The resulting lines can contain many sentences or simply a short snippet of text; we refer to them as \"paragraphs\"."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q258",
      "page": 34,
      "dimension": "input_form",
      "text": "To convert the raw web text in paragraph form to sentences, we apply language identification in a hierarchical fashion."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q259",
      "page": 34,
      "dimension": "input_form",
      "text": "First, we apply LID to each web paragraph."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q260",
      "page": 34,
      "dimension": "input_form",
      "text": "Subsequently, we use the predicted language to choose a sentence splitter for the language."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q261",
      "page": 34,
      "dimension": "input_form",
      "text": "The raw paragraphs sometimes contain a mix of different languages or might include code switching."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q262",
      "page": 34,
      "dimension": "input_form",
      "text": "To avoid having a mix of languages, once we have split the documents in sentences, we re-run LID to identify the language of each sentence."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q263",
      "page": 34,
      "dimension": "input_form",
      "text": "If the sentence-level LID does not match the paragraph-level LID, we discard the sentence to be sure we keep"
    },
    {
      "id": "Q264",
      "page": 35,
      "dimension": "input_form",
      "text": "We also discard sentences if they do not use the expected script for the target language."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q265",
      "page": 35,
      "dimension": "input_form",
      "text": "Note that many sentences are extremely noisy. In particular, they often contain long URLs or lists of hashtags. These confuse the LID and script identification process as they are in Latin script and not always in the same language as the original sentence."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q266",
      "page": 35,
      "dimension": "input_form",
      "text": "To identify the actual language of the sentence, we truncate the URLs and hashtags before running the language identification."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q267",
      "page": 35,
      "dimension": "input_content",
      "text": "Given the domain mismatch (see Section 5.1), our development set could not be utilized to tune the detection thresholds of our fasttext classifier to a desired performance level."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q268",
      "page": 35,
      "dimension": "input_content",
      "text": "Instead, we relied on the distribution of model scores on the monolingual data of the ParaCrawl dataset (Bañón et al., 2020) across all predicted languages."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q269",
      "page": 35,
      "dimension": "input_content",
      "text": "We chose that dataset based on the assumption that its language distribution would realistically match that of CommonCrawl, despite the inevitable bias induced by the LID model used in the creation of ParaCrawl itself."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q270",
      "page": 35,
      "dimension": "input_form",
      "text": "This analysis motivated our choice of 0.5 as a default threshold in the first two cases, except for high-resource languages, where we could afford a more stringent value of 0.9 and still collect enough monolingual data in our downstream pipeline depicted in Section 5.2. In the last case, we picked values corresponding to the peak of each distribution (ranging from 0.2 to 0.4), in the hope to collect a sizable amount of data from our pipeline."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q271",
      "page": 35,
      "dimension": "input_form",
      "text": "We subsequently apply a few heuristics to remove sentences that do not match reasonable quality criteria: minimum and maximum length, space/punctuation/number/emoji ratios, and maximum number of repeated characters."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q272",
      "page": 35,
      "dimension": "input_form",
      "text": "For example, if a sentence contains over 20% punctuation, it likely is not a well-formed sentence."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q273",
      "page": 35,
      "dimension": "input_form",
      "text": "As our model encoders (see Section 5.3) were not trained on substantial content with emojis, we prefer to strip emojis from all text to avoid losing sentences that could match if they did not have the special characters."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q274",
      "page": 36,
      "dimension": "input_form",
      "text": "Table 8: Examples of Filtered Sentences in our monolingual pipeline."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q275",
      "page": 36,
      "dimension": "input_form",
      "text": "We note that these ratios should differ between languages, and are not universally applicable. In certain languages, concepts may take many more words to convey, meaning that setting length-related thresholds is problematic. Similarly, other languages may utilize more punctuation or have shorter words. Thus, we do not set extremely stringent filters, and we examine the amount of text filtered across all 200 languages for each of the filters."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q276",
      "page": 36,
      "dimension": "input_form",
      "text": "Deduplication. The margin-based criterion of our mining approach requires unique sentences (see Section 5.3), but the sentence splitting and cleaning process might generate a lot of duplicate content, so we run a global deduplication process over all sentences of the same language."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q277",
      "page": 36,
      "dimension": "input_form",
      "text": "Language Model Filtering. As we are interested in keeping high quality sentences in our datasets to later train our final multilingual translation models, when possible, we also run a Language Model (LM) filtering. In practice, it is difficult to train high-quality language models for low-resource languages, so we focus on applying language model filters on a few high-resource languages only. Because we do most of the mining where one side of the pair is English, we believe that if we have high-quality content in the English corpus, the mining alignment process will also output high-quality content on the other side of the pair. For English, we use the KenLM (Heafield, 2011) model from CCNet (Wenzek et al., 2020)."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q278",
      "page": 36,
      "dimension": "input_content",
      "text": "We processed around 37.7 Petabytes of data through the whole pipeline. This was a challenge for data management and disk usage. In particular, we had to make hard decisions when filtering high-resource languages to artificially keep only around 30% of data from the most voluminous languages. This threshold was identified as the limit under which the LM score would identify sentences of low quality."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q279",
      "page": 36,
      "dimension": "input_content",
      "text": "We realize that processing such volume of data is not always possible and are open-sourcing much of our results and code to make it easier for everyone to benefit from our effort."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q280",
      "page": 36,
      "dimension": "input_content",
      "text": "We started with 107.9 billion paragraphs from the web (97.4% high-resource, 2.6% low-resource) and discarded 2.8 billion sentences (85.3% high, 14.7% low) because of LID/Script mismatch or low LID score (see Section 5.1) to produce 43.7 billion monolingual sentences, of which 21.5 billion sentences are in English."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q281",
      "page": 37,
      "dimension": "input_form",
      "text": "Note that we have such a big drop in number of sentences because we drastically filtered high-resource languages to keep the top 30% of sentences based on LM score."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q282",
      "page": 37,
      "dimension": "input_ontology",
      "text": "Machine translation, like many machine learning applications, is heavily data-driven."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q283",
      "page": 37,
      "dimension": "input_content",
      "text": "Previous works have clearly established that translation quality generally increases with the amount of available high-quality training data (Koehn and Knowles, 2017)."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q284",
      "page": 37,
      "dimension": "input_content",
      "text": "Existing parallel corpora for low-resource languages are often opportunistically drawn from known collections of multilingual content, such as the Christian Bible or publications of multinational organizations."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q285",
      "page": 37,
      "dimension": "input_content",
      "text": "These are often limited in quantity and domain."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q286",
      "page": 37,
      "dimension": "input_ontology",
      "text": "The underlying idea of our bitext mining approach is to first learn a multilingual sentence embedding space and to use a similarity measure in that space to decide whether two sentences are parallel or not."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q287",
      "page": 37,
      "dimension": "input_ontology",
      "text": "This comparison can be done for all possible pairs in two collections of monolingual texts, termed global mining in Schwenk et al. (2021a)."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q288",
      "page": 37,
      "dimension": "input_ontology",
      "text": "Another common alternative approach is referred to as hierarchical or local mining and comprises of first performing a selection of potential document pairs, and then limiting the mining to sentences within each document pair."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q289",
      "page": 37,
      "dimension": "input_ontology",
      "text": "In this work we follow the approach from WikiMatrix (Schwenk et al., 2021a) and CCMatrix (Schwenk et al., 2021b), which both used global mining."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q290",
      "page": 37,
      "dimension": "input_content",
      "text": "As our mining approach requires a multilingual embedding space, we faced several challenges when scaling this representation to the 200 languages of the No Language Left Behind effort."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q291",
      "page": 37,
      "dimension": "input_content",
      "text": "For example, how do we make sure that all languages are well-learned? And how should we account for large imbalances of available training data?"
    },
    {
      "id": "Q292",
      "page": 37,
      "dimension": "input_ontology",
      "text": "Training a massively multilingual sentence encoder from scratch each time a new set of languages is added would be computationally very expensive."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q293",
      "page": 38,
      "dimension": "input_ontology",
      "text": "the drawback that the learned embedding spaces from each new model are not (naturally) mutually compatible. This can make mining intractable as for each new encoder, the entirety of available monolingual data needs to be re-embedded, and for English alone, this means tens of billions of sentences and large compute resources."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q294",
      "page": 38,
      "dimension": "input_ontology",
      "text": "In order to overcome these issues, one approach is to train smaller mutually compatible sentence encoders using the teacher-student distillation technique proposed by Reimers and Gurevych (2020)."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q295",
      "page": 38,
      "dimension": "input_ontology",
      "text": "Several extensions of this underlying idea were proposed by Heffernan et al. (2022) that we adopt (see Section 5.3.2)."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q296",
      "page": 38,
      "dimension": "input_ontology",
      "text": "In order to find aligned texts, early approaches focused on information beyond the text itself."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q297",
      "page": 38,
      "dimension": "input_ontology",
      "text": "More recent approaches have begun to leverage advancements in representation learning by encoding texts into an embedding space, and then using a distance-based method to determine if a pair of texts in different languages have a similar meaning."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q298",
      "page": 38,
      "dimension": "input_ontology",
      "text": "Works such as España-Bonet et al. (2017); Guo et al. (2018); Hassan et al. (2018); Yang et al. (2019) used bilingual embeddings, but this has the limitation of not being able to directly mine across many languages."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q299",
      "page": 38,
      "dimension": "input_ontology",
      "text": "In order to address this, learning a massively multilingual embedding space allows for any pair of languages to be encoded and mined (Artetxe and Schwenk, 2019a,b; Feng et al., 2020; Kvapilíková et al., 2020; Schwenk, 2018)."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q300",
      "page": 38,
      "dimension": "output_form",
      "text": "However, when applying these approaches to obtain representations at the sentence level, they can often suffer from the lack of an explicit sentence-based criterion during training, resulting in poor performance on tasks such as bitext retrieval (Hu et al., 2020)."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q301",
      "page": 39,
      "dimension": "input_form",
      "text": "However, pre-training for the BERT encoders is done using both a masked language modelling (MLM) and translation language modelling (TLM) objective (Conneau et al., 2020)."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q302",
      "page": 39,
      "dimension": "output_ontology",
      "text": "Sentence embeddings are then produced by passing bilingual translation pairs through the dual-encoder setup and then applying an additive margin softmax loss (Yang et al., 2019)."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q303",
      "page": 39,
      "dimension": "input_form",
      "text": "Unlike the previous BERT-based approaches, there is no pre-training, and sentence embeddings are produced by using an encoder-decoder architecture, and then max-pooling over the encoder outputs."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q304",
      "page": 39,
      "dimension": "input_ontology",
      "text": "When attempting to learn a multilingual embedding space, one of the limitations of many existing approaches is that each time a model is to be expanded to include a new set of languages, the entire model must be retrained from scratch, which is very costly."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q305",
      "page": 39,
      "dimension": "input_content",
      "text": "In this distillation setup, English-paired bitexts are used to both learn the English embedding space of a monolingual teacher (SBERT), while also using the non-English side to learn a new language."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q306",
      "page": 39,
      "dimension": "input_ontology",
      "text": "Heffernan et al. (2022) further built upon this approach by experimenting with different architectures for teacher and student (e.g., BiLSTM and Transformer), and also applying such distilled sentence representations to the task of bitext mining."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q307",
      "page": 39,
      "dimension": "input_ontology",
      "text": "The overall approach focuses on starting with a massively multilingual sentence encoder teacher model and adapting it to several different low-resource student models."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q308",
      "page": 39,
      "dimension": "input_ontology",
      "text": "This enables us to add low-resource languages without needing to compete with high-resource languages for capacity, to avoid retraining the full model from scratch, and to maintain compatibility of the multilingual embedding spaces for subsequent mining."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q309",
      "page": 40,
      "dimension": "input_form",
      "text": "The original training procedure (Artetxe and Schwenk, 2019b) was changed as follows: the use of SentencePiece tokenization and upsampling of low-resource languages."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q310",
      "page": 40,
      "dimension": "input_content",
      "text": "Training was performed on the same 93 languages with public resources obtained from OPUS (Tiedemann, 2012)."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q311",
      "page": 40,
      "dimension": "input_ontology",
      "text": "students are specialized for one language or several similar languages;"
    },
    {
      "id": "Q312",
      "page": 40,
      "dimension": "input_ontology",
      "text": "students are randomly initialized since we want to handle low-resource language for which we don't have a pre-trained LM;"
    },
    {
      "id": "Q313",
      "page": 40,
      "dimension": "input_form",
      "text": "students may have a dedicated SentencePiece vocabulary different from the teacher, to better accommodate scripts and tokens in the student languages (see Section 5.3.3)"
    },
    {
      "id": "Q314",
      "page": 40,
      "dimension": "output_ontology",
      "text": "students learn to minimize the cosine loss with the teacher, since we also use cosine distance for bitext mining (see Figure 12);"
    },
    {
      "id": "Q315",
      "page": 40,
      "dimension": "output_ontology",
      "text": "students can have an MLM loss to leverage student language monolingual data (see Figure 12 and Section 5.3.3)."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q316",
      "page": 40,
      "dimension": "input_ontology",
      "text": "Our student encoders used a 12-layer transformer, hidden size of 1024, with 4 attention heads, totalling around 250M parameters."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q317",
      "page": 40,
      "dimension": "input_content",
      "text": "All students were trained with available bitexts in their respective language, complemented by two million sentences of English/English and English/Spanish."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q318",
      "page": 40,
      "dimension": "input_ontology",
      "text": "Teacher-student training was performed on 16 GPUs, ADAM optimizer, a learning rate of 0.0005, and a batch size of 10,000."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q319",
      "page": 40,
      "dimension": "input_ontology",
      "text": "We trained student encoders for 148 languages and named these models LASER3."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q320",
      "page": 40,
      "dimension": "input_ontology",
      "text": "Mined bitexts will be subsequently utilized to improve translation quality for 200 languages."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q321",
      "page": 40,
      "dimension": "output_form",
      "text": "Consequently, our primary metric is neural machine translation (NMT) quality."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q322",
      "page": 40,
      "dimension": "output_form",
      "text": "However, mining and NMT training are computationally expensive, and it is intractable to systematically perform this evaluation for many different sentence encoder variants."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q323",
      "page": 40,
      "dimension": "output_form",
      "text": "As an evaluation proxy, we use a mining-based multilingual similarity search error rate, referred to here as xsim."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q324",
      "page": 40,
      "dimension": "output_form",
      "text": "As opposed to cosine accuracy which aligns embeddings based on the highest cosine score, xsim aligns source and target embeddings based on the highest margin score, which was shown to be beneficial in mining (Artetxe and Schwenk, 2019a)."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q325",
      "page": 41,
      "dimension": "output_form",
      "text": "where x and y are the source and target sentences, and NNk(x) denotes the k nearest neighbors of x in the other language. We set k to 4."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q326",
      "page": 41,
      "dimension": "output_form",
      "text": "All xsim results are calculated on Flores-200 devtest, using the ratio margin where margin(a, b) = a/b."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q327",
      "page": 41,
      "dimension": "output_form",
      "text": "Additionally, all scores are calculated into English (i.e. xxx → eng). English is encoded by the teacher and the other language by the LASER3 student."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q328",
      "page": 41,
      "dimension": "output_form",
      "text": "Initial experiments indicated that a threshold on the margin of 1.06 seems to be the best compromise between precision and recall for most of the languages."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q329",
      "page": 41,
      "dimension": "input_form",
      "text": "For these NMT baselines, we do not apply additional filtering on the bitexts and leave this to the training procedure of our massively multilingual NMT system."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q330",
      "page": 41,
      "dimension": "output_form",
      "text": "We further limit our experimentation to the translation from foreign languages into English. This helps to compare resources and assess the translation quality among all languages."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q331",
      "page": 41,
      "dimension": "input_content",
      "text": "The English corpus we mine in has 21.5 billion unique sentences."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q332",
      "page": 41,
      "dimension": "output_form",
      "text": "We do not attempt to optimize the architecture and parameters of the bilingual NMT systems to the characteristics of each language pair, namely the size of available bitexts, but use the same architecture for all."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q333",
      "page": 41,
      "dimension": "output_form",
      "text": "Therefore, the reported results should not be interpreted as the best possible ones given the available resources – they are mainly provided to validate the mined bitexts."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q334",
      "page": 41,
      "dimension": "input_form",
      "text": "We use a 12 layer encoder and decoder and train for 100 epochs."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q335",
      "page": 41,
      "dimension": "input_form",
      "text": "The SentencePiece (SPM) vocabulary has 7,000 tokens."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q336",
      "page": 41,
      "dimension": "output_form",
      "text": "We look for best performance on the Flores-200 development set, and report detokenized BLEU on Flores-200 devtest."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q337",
      "page": 41,
      "dimension": "input_content",
      "text": "The original LASER encoder, as used in the CCMatrix project (Schwenk et al., 2021b) performs very well on several high-resource languages like Arabic, Chinese, Czech, German, Japanese, Polish or Indonesian."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q338",
      "page": 41,
      "dimension": "input_content",
      "text": "We used the CCMatrix bitexts directly for these languages. We then trained new sentence encoders and performed mining for the 148 remaining ones."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q339",
      "page": 41,
      "dimension": "output_form",
      "text": "On average the xsim error is brought down from 61 to 0.91."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q340",
      "page": 41,
      "dimension": "output_form",
      "text": "In particular, some languages such as Burmese (mya_Mymr) and Irish (gle_Latn) saw the biggest reductions in xsim, with decreases of 93.3 → 0.89 and 92.5 → 0.79, respectively."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q341",
      "page": 41,
      "dimension": "input_ontology",
      "text": "There is a large variety of languages which are spoken locally in various regions of Europe. We consider here 10 languages."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q342",
      "page": 41,
      "dimension": "input_content",
      "text": "For most of them, we were not able to find meaningful amounts of public bitexts and heavily utilize NLLB-Seed"
    },
    {
      "id": "Q343",
      "page": 42,
      "dimension": "input_content",
      "text": "Therefore, we chose to train individual sentence encoders specific to each of these languages and complemented the training data with 2M bitexts in a similar higher-resource European languages."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q344",
      "page": 42,
      "dimension": "input_content",
      "text": "Typical examples are Sicilian paired with Italian or Silesian paired with Polish."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q345",
      "page": 42,
      "dimension": "output_form",
      "text": "We observe that pairing the minority language with another similar major language yields encoders with very low xsim error rates for most of the languages, and we were able to mine large amounts of bitexts yielding good NMT performance."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q346",
      "page": 42,
      "dimension": "output_form",
      "text": "Three languages reach a BLEU score superior to 20 (fur_Latn, lmo_Latn and srd_Latn), and two languages superior to 30 (ltz_Latn and ydd_Hebr)."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q347",
      "page": 42,
      "dimension": "input_ontology",
      "text": "We applied a similar strategy for Creole languages."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q348",
      "page": 42,
      "dimension": "input_ontology",
      "text": "Linguistically speaking, Creole languages are a possible outcome of a contact situation between languages over a fairly brief period of time (Lent et al., 2022)."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q349",
      "page": 42,
      "dimension": "input_content",
      "text": "When training the sentence encoders, we paired each Creole language with a \"similar\" high-resource language (see Table 11)."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q350",
      "page": 42,
      "dimension": "input_content",
      "text": "The sentence encoders have a very low xsim error rate for all languages except Sango (sag_Latn) for which we were not able to identify a similar language with sufficient resources."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q351",
      "page": 43,
      "dimension": "input_content",
      "text": "For the former, we were able to crawl 28M sentences of monolingual data, while we have less than 300k for the latter."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q352",
      "page": 43,
      "dimension": "input_content",
      "text": "Both have less than ten thousand sentences of existing bitexts which is largely insufficient to train an NMT system."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q353",
      "page": 43,
      "dimension": "output_form",
      "text": "We were able to mine more than 7M bitexts for Papiamento which yielded an impressive BLEU score of 40.9, while we only achieve BLEU 4.9 for Kabuverdianu."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q354",
      "page": 43,
      "dimension": "input_content",
      "text": "This highlights that the amount of available monolingual data is crucial to make bitext mining successful."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q355",
      "page": 43,
      "dimension": "input_ontology",
      "text": "We considered several languages of the Berber family, namely Kabyle (kab_Latn), Tamashek (taq) and Central Atlas Tamazight (tzm)."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q356",
      "page": 43,
      "dimension": "input_form",
      "text": "We consider Tamazight written in the Tifinagh script and Tamashek both in Latin and Tifinagh script."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q357",
      "page": 43,
      "dimension": "input_content",
      "text": "All are very low-resource languages with barely 10,000 sentences of available bitext, and 72,000 for Kabyle."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q358",
      "page": 43,
      "dimension": "input_content",
      "text": "It was also very challenging to collect monolingual data for these Berber languages."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q359",
      "page": 43,
      "dimension": "output_form",
      "text": "xsim error rates for Tamashek are above 20% and insufficient amount of monolingual data make it impossible to mine bitext of good quality for Tamashek."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q360",
      "page": 43,
      "dimension": "input_content",
      "text": "Tamashek and Tamazight are typical examples of very low-resource languages for which it seems to be very hard to collect written material to support training of machine translation system."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q361",
      "page": 43,
      "dimension": "input_ontology",
      "text": "We discuss here 13 languages from this family, and use a single encoder for ten of them."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q362",
      "page": 43,
      "dimension": "input_ontology",
      "text": "The languages Fijian, Maori, and Samoan are handled by a separate encoder."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q363",
      "page": 43,
      "dimension": "output_form",
      "text": "We observe very low xsim error rates for most of the languages, although several languages have less than hundred thousand sentences of bitexts."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q364",
      "page": 43,
      "dimension": "input_ontology",
      "text": "Training all languages together in one specific encoder for this family seems to be very beneficial for these very low-resource languages."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q365",
      "page": 43,
      "dimension": "input_content",
      "text": "In addition, we were able to collect several million sentences of monolingual text for most of the languages."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q366",
      "page": 43,
      "dimension": "output_form",
      "text": "This gives us optimal conditions for mining and we achieve substantial improvements in the BLEU score compared to training a bilingual NMT system on the public bitexts only."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q367",
      "page": 44,
      "dimension": "input_ontology",
      "text": "Among the 200 languages of the NLLB project, 55 are spoken in the African continent, which is more than a quarter of all languages we handle."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q368",
      "page": 44,
      "dimension": "input_content",
      "text": "Except for seven languages — Modern Standard Arabic, Afrikaans, Southern Sotho, Swahili, Tswana, Xhosa and Zulu — all are low-resource languages, i.e. with less than one million publicly available sentence pairs."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q369",
      "page": 44,
      "dimension": "input_content",
      "text": "Twelve of them even have less than hundred thousand sentence pairs, which we named very low-resource languages."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q370",
      "page": 44,
      "dimension": "input_content",
      "text": "In addition, we struggled to curate meaningful amounts of monolingual data."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q371",
      "page": 44,
      "dimension": "input_content",
      "text": "Given these facts, training sentence encoders for African languages and mining high quality bitexts turned out to be a major challenge — even in the broader community."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q372",
      "page": 44,
      "dimension": "output_form",
      "text": "The average BLEU score over 44 languages increased from 11.0 to 14.8 with help of the mined bitexts."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q373",
      "page": 44,
      "dimension": "input_form",
      "text": "We also deployed a new training procedure which combines supervised training, i.e. minimizing the cosine loss between the teacher and student embedding, and unsupervised masked LM training (see left part of Figure 12)."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q374",
      "page": 44,
      "dimension": "input_form",
      "text": "This enabled us to benefit from monolingual data during encoder training."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q375",
      "page": 44,
      "dimension": "output_content",
      "text": "A detailed description and analysis of our effort is reported in Heffernan et al. (2022)."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q376",
      "page": 45,
      "dimension": "output_form",
      "text": "Table 14: xsim Error Rates on FLORES devtest for Amharic and Tigrinya and different training strategies. The specified amount of training data excludes 4M sentences of English for our models."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q377",
      "page": 45,
      "dimension": "input_form",
      "text": "In massively multilingual systems, a common approach is to utilize the same SentencePiece vocabulary."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q378",
      "page": 45,
      "dimension": "input_form",
      "text": "In our initial experimentation, we re-used the LASER2 teacher 50k vocabulary for all student encoders."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q379",
      "page": 45,
      "dimension": "input_form",
      "text": "However, despite upsampling, low-resource languages could be poorly represented in a joint vocabulary."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q380",
      "page": 45,
      "dimension": "input_form",
      "text": "We next explore utilizing specific vocabularies for small subsets of languages."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q381",
      "page": 45,
      "dimension": "input_ontology",
      "text": "We first explore training an encoder for three Semitic languages: Amharic, Tigrinya, and Maltese."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q382",
      "page": 45,
      "dimension": "input_form",
      "text": "We then trained an encoder for Amharic and Tigrinya only, paired with English as in all our experiments, and a specific 8k SentencePiece vocabulary to better support the Ge'ez script."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q383",
      "page": 45,
      "dimension": "input_content",
      "text": "Overall, we mined 148 bitexts paired with English which totals to 761 million sentence pairs with an alignment score of at least 1.06."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q384",
      "page": 45,
      "dimension": "input_content",
      "text": "Bitexts aligned with English for the remaining languages were taken from CCMatrix (Schwenk et al., 2021b)."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q385",
      "page": 45,
      "dimension": "input_content",
      "text": "We also provide 1465 non-English bitext pairs. This corresponds to 302 million sentence pairs. This includes all language pairs among African, Indic and Malayo-Polynesian families, respectively, as well as alignments of all African languages with French."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q386",
      "page": 45,
      "dimension": "input_content",
      "text": "We note that for some languages, we are only able to create a small amount of bitext through data mining. The limiting factor is predominantly the lack of monolingual data."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q387",
      "page": 45,
      "dimension": "input_content",
      "text": "Many low-resource languages have limited presence on the web, and the data that we curate can be heavily filtered at many stages: language identification, aggressive cleaning of monolingual data, or even poorly aligned bitext."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q388",
      "page": 45,
      "dimension": "input_content",
      "text": "Even with our best efforts, those challenges compound, and they can affect certain languages far more than others."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q389",
      "page": 45,
      "dimension": "input_content",
      "text": "Further, note that even in our mined bitext, we still end up including some content that is already available from"
    },
    {
      "id": "Q390",
      "page": 46,
      "dimension": "input_content",
      "text": "An important final consideration is the web already has machine translated content. For example, many websites may use translation to 'internationalize' their content. A positive is that a large majority of the languages we focus on are not contained in most existing commercial translation services (see Table 1), however as we mine against higher-resource languages, it is likely our mined datasets contain translated content."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q391",
      "page": 46,
      "dimension": "input_content",
      "text": "While we performed our due diligence on deployments of all licensed datasets, the ownership of low-resource language data remains an open debate."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q392",
      "page": 46,
      "dimension": "output_content",
      "text": "In our interview study, many low-resource stakeholders express that sharing language access might in fact be a necessary trade-off for technological advancement."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q393",
      "page": 46,
      "dimension": "input_content",
      "text": "Even though we deploy many low-resource language datasets, ownership ultimately belongs to the speakers of these languages."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q394",
      "page": 46,
      "dimension": "input_content",
      "text": "We describe our methodology for automatically creating aligned translation training data for low-resource languages. We face significant challenges, as bitext data to train sentence encoders such as LASER and monolingual data to mine in is extremely scarce."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q395",
      "page": 46,
      "dimension": "input_ontology",
      "text": "we develop (1) a high-quality language identification system for over 200 languages that outperforms publicly available LIDs in both Flores-200 and web domains, (2) a detailed, documented monolingual dataset curation and cleaning pipeline, and (3) a teacher-student based multilingual sentence encoder training methodology that enables transfer to extremely low-resource languages with minimal supervised bitext. These contributions combine to create over 1.1 billion new sentence pairs of training data for 148 languages."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q396",
      "page": 46,
      "dimension": "input_content",
      "text": "We are releasing all the code that was used to train the LID model, and run the monolingual sentence splitting and filtering. We are also releasing the mining code, under an open source license, with tools to run mining with our open-sourced LASER encoders."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q397",
      "page": 47,
      "dimension": "input_ontology",
      "text": "Existing research in massively multilingual machine translation has been predominantly restricted to about 100 languages, which represent only a fraction of globally written languages (Arivazhagan et al., 2019; Fan et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2020)."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q398",
      "page": 47,
      "dimension": "output_form",
      "text": "Some works have extended beyond (Mueller et al., 2020; Siddhant et al., 2022), but critically lack reliable performance evaluation."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q399",
      "page": 47,
      "dimension": "output_form",
      "text": "Despite much research, the translation quality for languages with low volumes of data is typically poor."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q400",
      "page": 47,
      "dimension": "input_content",
      "text": "Further, adding extremely low-resource languages beyond 100 is very challenging because there is often very little existing good quality available bitext, and even large scale bitext mining (Schwenk et al., 2021b) can struggle to create sufficiently large datasets (see Section 5.3)."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q401",
      "page": 47,
      "dimension": "input_content",
      "text": "Data often varies widely in available volume across languages, creating imbalance between different language directions."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q402",
      "page": 47,
      "dimension": "input_content",
      "text": "This complicates massively multilingual training, as some language directions have begun overfitting while others have not yet even converged."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q403",
      "page": 47,
      "dimension": "input_ontology",
      "text": "We develop several novel techniques that tackle the major challenges of low-resource translation, such as training models with sufficient capacity to represent 200+ languages while adjusting to variable data capacity per language pair."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q404",
      "page": 47,
      "dimension": "input_ontology",
      "text": "These involve (1) conditional compute models to minimize interference between unrelated language directions, (2) studying the best self-supervision strategies on monolingual data, and (3)"
    },
    {
      "id": "Q405",
      "page": 48,
      "dimension": "input_ontology",
      "text": "We model multilingual neural machine translation as a sequence-to-sequence task, where we condition on an input sequence in the source language with an encoder and generate the output sequence in the expected target language with a decoder (Bahdanau et al., 2015)."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q406",
      "page": 48,
      "dimension": "output_ontology",
      "text": "We train to maximize the probability of the translation in the target language T, given the source sentence S, the source language ℓs, and the target language ℓt, i.e., P(T|S, ℓs, ℓt)."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q407",
      "page": 48,
      "dimension": "input_form",
      "text": "To tokenize our text sequences, we train a single SentencePiece (SPM) (Kudo and Richardson, 2018) model for all languages."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q408",
      "page": 48,
      "dimension": "input_content",
      "text": "We sample a total of 100M sentences from primary bitext data."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q409",
      "page": 48,
      "dimension": "input_form",
      "text": "To ensure low-resource languages are well-represented in the vocabulary, we downsample high-resource and upsample low-resource languages with a sampling temperature of 5 (Arivazhagan et al., 2019)."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q410",
      "page": 48,
      "dimension": "input_form",
      "text": "Vocabulary size is a critical hyperparameter in multilingual translation models involving low-resource languages (Oladipo et al., 2022; Rajab, 2022)."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q411",
      "page": 48,
      "dimension": "input_form",
      "text": "The vocabulary size of our trained SPM model is 256,000."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q412",
      "page": 48,
      "dimension": "input_ontology",
      "text": "Our sequence-to-sequence multilingual machine translation model is based on the Transformer encoder-decoder architecture (Vaswani et al., 2017)."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q413",
      "page": 48,
      "dimension": "input_form",
      "text": "Note that we prefix the source sequence with the source language, as opposed to the target language as previously done in several works (Arivazhagan et al., 2019; Johnson et al., 2017)."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q414",
      "page": 48,
      "dimension": "input_ontology",
      "text": "This is primarily because we prioritize optimizing zero-shot performance of our model on any pair of 200 languages at a minor cost to supervised performance."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q415",
      "page": 48,
      "dimension": "input_ontology",
      "text": "Empirically, we find zero-shot performance to be negatively affected when conditioning the encoder on"
    },
    {
      "id": "Q416",
      "page": 49,
      "dimension": "input_ontology",
      "text": "We construct a multilingual machine translation benchmark such that it is representative of our final benchmark on 200+ languages."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q417",
      "page": 49,
      "dimension": "input_ontology",
      "text": "We choose a representative sub-sample of 53 out of 202 languages and a total of 110 translation directions (see Table 51 in the appendix)."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q418",
      "page": 49,
      "dimension": "input_ontology",
      "text": "These consist of 45 directions out of English (aggregated as eng_Latn-xx), 45 directions into English (aggregated as xx-eng_Latn) and 20 non-English directions (aggregated as xx-yy)."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q419",
      "page": 49,
      "dimension": "input_ontology",
      "text": "In terms of resource level, there are 40 high-resource and 70 low-resource directions (see Table 1 and Table 51)."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q420",
      "page": 49,
      "dimension": "input_ontology",
      "text": "Out of 70 low-resource directions, 22 are very low-resource, i.e., have less than 100K training examples."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q421",
      "page": 49,
      "dimension": "input_content",
      "text": "The dataset is composed of publicly available bitext in all 110 language directions (see Section 8.1.2) and large scale mined data (see Section 5.3)"
    },
    {
      "id": "Q422",
      "page": 49,
      "dimension": "input_form",
      "text": "Ablation Dataset Counts depicting the amount of training data across all language pairs, ranking from 39,992 to 18.7 million sentence pairs."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q423",
      "page": 50,
      "dimension": "input_content",
      "text": "There are a total of 864M examples in this benchmark."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q424",
      "page": 50,
      "dimension": "input_content",
      "text": "The highest resource language pair has 186M examples and the lowest resource language pair has 40K examples, thus representing the extreme skew characteristic of the final dataset with 202 languages."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q425",
      "page": 50,
      "dimension": "input_content",
      "text": "Figure 15 shows the data distribution over language pairs sorted by the example count per pair."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q426",
      "page": 50,
      "dimension": "input_ontology",
      "text": "We call this dataset our ablation dataset and use this throughout all experiments in this section."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q427",
      "page": 50,
      "dimension": "input_content",
      "text": "For this ablation dataset, we only include English-centric data to manage experimental iteration speed."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q428",
      "page": 50,
      "dimension": "input_ontology",
      "text": "A massively multilingual translation model is trained on several translation directions at once, utilizing the same shared model capacity."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q429",
      "page": 50,
      "dimension": "input_ontology",
      "text": "This can lead to beneficial crosslingual transfer between related languages at the risk of increasing interference between unrelated languages."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q430",
      "page": 50,
      "dimension": "input_ontology",
      "text": "Sparsely Gated Mixture of Experts (MoE) models are a type of conditional compute models that activate a subset of model parameters per input, as opposed to dense models that activate all model parameters per input."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q431",
      "page": 50,
      "dimension": "input_ontology",
      "text": "We follow the Top-k-Gating algorithm of Lepikhin et al. (2020) and dispatch each token to at most k = 2 experts."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q432",
      "page": 50,
      "dimension": "input_ontology",
      "text": "We always choose the top 2 scoring experts per token, and do not add randomization to the choice of the second expert."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q433",
      "page": 51,
      "dimension": "input_ontology",
      "text": "The Transformer encoder-decoder model, supplemented with MoE layers and their respective gating networks, learns to route input tokens to the corresponding top-2 experts by optimizing a linearly weighted combination of label-smoothed cross entropy (Szegedy et al., 2015) and an auxiliary load balancing loss (Shazeer et al., 2017)."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q434",
      "page": 51,
      "dimension": "output_form",
      "text": "This additional loss term (LB) pushes the tokens to be uniformly distributed across experts and is evaluated as: LB = E · ∑ E e=1 fe pe, pe = 1/T · ∑ T t=1 Gt e, where fe is the fraction of tokens routed to the eth expert, as their first choice, through Top-k-Gating, and pe is the average routing probability to that expert over the T tokens in the mini-batch."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q435",
      "page": 51,
      "dimension": "input_ontology",
      "text": "In the rest of this section, we first detail how we train vanilla Sparsely Gated MoE models for multilingual machine translation on our benchmark and show how they compare to dense models."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q436",
      "page": 51,
      "dimension": "input_ontology",
      "text": "We then discuss why these vanilla Sparsely Gated MoE models are suboptimal for low-resource language pairs (Section 6.2.1)."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q437",
      "page": 51,
      "dimension": "input_ontology",
      "text": "We propose in Section 6.2.2 a series of architectural changes that significantly improve the performance on low-resource language pairs with MoE models."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q438",
      "page": 52,
      "dimension": "input_ontology",
      "text": "We train a baseline dense Transformer encoder-decoder model with 1.3B parameters with model dimension 1024, FFN dimension 8192, 16 attention heads, 24 encoder layers and 24 decoder layers."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q439",
      "page": 52,
      "dimension": "input_ontology",
      "text": "Next, we train a corresponding Sparsely Gated MoE model by replacing the dense FFN sublayer with an MoE sublayer in every alternate"
    },
    {
      "id": "Q440",
      "page": 52,
      "dimension": "output_form",
      "text": "We report averages in each set of directions: eng_Latn-xx, xx-eng_Latn and xx-yy as all."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q441",
      "page": 52,
      "dimension": "output_form",
      "text": "For eng_Latn-xx and xx-eng_Latn we breakdown the pairs by resource level: high-resource (high), low-resource (low) and very low resource (v.low)"
    },
    {
      "id": "Q442",
      "page": 52,
      "dimension": "output_form",
      "text": "We see that a vanilla MoE model does not outperform the corresponding 1.3B dense model on the ablation benchmark."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q443",
      "page": 52,
      "dimension": "output_form",
      "text": "On adding overall dropout, we see a significant improvement in all directions on MoE models."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q444",
      "page": 52,
      "dimension": "output_form",
      "text": "At smaller computational cost per update (615M), MoE with overall dropout shows larger gains."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q445",
      "page": 52,
      "dimension": "input_ontology",
      "text": "The motivation behind sparsely activating expert subnetworks in an MoE model is to allow different parameters to model different aspects of the input space."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q446",
      "page": 52,
      "dimension": "input_ontology",
      "text": "We hypothesize that the added expert capacity should help higher resource language pairs that might otherwise be constrained to share the same dense model capacity with many other language pairs."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q447",
      "page": 52,
      "dimension": "input_ontology",
      "text": "We also hypothesize that with a massive number of translation directions, the added expert capacity would reduce interference, thus benefiting tasks of all resource levels."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q448",
      "page": 53,
      "dimension": "input_ontology",
      "text": "Each MoE sublayer has 64 experts (close to the number of languages in the benchmark, i.e., 53) and routes input tokens to the top-2 expert FFN sublayers in the MoE layer as in Lepikhin et al. (2020)."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q449",
      "page": 53,
      "dimension": "input_form",
      "text": "All models are trained for 100k updates with an effective batch size of 1M tokens per update."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q450",
      "page": 53,
      "dimension": "output_form",
      "text": "For dense models, the objective function is label-smoothed cross-entropy (ε = 0.1) (Szegedy et al., 2015), and for MoE models, the objective function is a weighted sum of label-smoothed cross-entropy and the load balancing loss (Equation (9)) with weights 1.0 and 0.01, respectively."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q451",
      "page": 53,
      "dimension": "input_form",
      "text": "We optimize with Adam (Kingma and Ba, 2015) using (β1, β2, ε) = (0.9, 0.98, 10−6)."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q452",
      "page": 53,
      "dimension": "input_form",
      "text": "We linearly increase the learning rate up to 0.004 through 8000 warmup updates, then follow the inverse square root learning rate schedule."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q453",
      "page": 53,
      "dimension": "input_form",
      "text": "For Top-2-Gating, we set the expert capacity to 2 × T/E, i.e., we enforce that each expert processes, at most, 2 × T/E tokens, where T is the number of tokens in the mini-batch and E is the number of experts."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q454",
      "page": 53,
      "dimension": "input_form",
      "text": "During generation, we set the capacity to T so that all tokens can be routed to whichever expert they choose."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q455",
      "page": 53,
      "dimension": "output_form",
      "text": "We use the chrF++ metric to compare the model performance (see Section 7.1)."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q456",
      "page": 53,
      "dimension": "output_form",
      "text": "We see 1+ chrF++ score improvements on all subsets except for very low resource pairs (v.low) and non-English pairs (xx-yy)."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q457",
      "page": 53,
      "dimension": "output_form",
      "text": "Adding overall dropout (sweeping over pdrop∈{0.1, 0.2, 0.3}) significantly improves the performance of MoE-64 in both the 615M and 1.3B variants."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q458",
      "page": 53,
      "dimension": "input_content",
      "text": "We hypothesize two potential reasons for this: (1) we use a temperature of 1.0 for sampling, i.e., we do not upsample datasets from low-resource pairs."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q459",
      "page": 53,
      "dimension": "input_content",
      "text": "As we increase computational cost per update, the propensity for low or very low-resource pairs to overfit increases thus causing performance to deteriorate."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q460",
      "page": 53,
      "dimension": "input_content",
      "text": "We observe in the case of eng_Latn-kon_Latn, a very low-resource pair, that the model continues to face significant overfitting when trained for 100k updates."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q461",
      "page": 53,
      "dimension": "input_content",
      "text": "This is unsurprising, as iterating over a small training set with large capacity causes overfitting."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q462",
      "page": 54,
      "dimension": "input_content",
      "text": "Although overall dropout is sufficient to regularize dense models, MoE models with overall dropout still significantly overfit on low-resource pairs as seen in Figure 17."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q463",
      "page": 54,
      "dimension": "input_content",
      "text": "MoE models enable specialized expert capacity to be activated based on the input token. However, with increased capacity, the learned token-expert assignment can cause the models to overfit, especially on low-resource translation directions."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q464",
      "page": 54,
      "dimension": "input_ontology",
      "text": "In this proposed regularization strategy, we mask the expert output for a random fraction (peom) of the input tokens."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q465",
      "page": 54,
      "dimension": "input_ontology",
      "text": "For input tokens with dropped expert outputs, the first and/or second expert is effectively skipped."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q466",
      "page": 54,
      "dimension": "input_ontology",
      "text": "Note that although this masking will zero out some combination weights Gt,e in Equation (13), it will not affect the weights used in the load balancing loss in Equation (9)."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q467",
      "page": 54,
      "dimension": "input_ontology",
      "text": "We compare EOM to Gating Dropout (Liu et al., 2022), a strategy for reducing cross-machine communication in MoE layers which also has a regularizing effect."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q468",
      "page": 55,
      "dimension": "input_ontology",
      "text": "Figure 18: Illustration of MoE Expert Output Masking in contrast to overall dropout for MoE layers: a color represents a token, and each token is dispatched to two experts (Top-k-Gating). Faded colors correspond to dropped units or masked outputs."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q469",
      "page": 55,
      "dimension": "input_ontology",
      "text": "skips the All-to-All communication between GPUs with probability pgd, routing tokens to the local experts instead."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q470",
      "page": 55,
      "dimension": "input_ontology",
      "text": "Final Output Masking (FOM). A simpler alternative to EOM would be to mask the combined expert output for a random fraction of tokens, i.e., after the last stage in Figure 18b. We denote with pfom the fraction of tokens masked with this regularization method. Note that this type of masking is more generic as it can be applied to dense models as well — in testing it here, we validate the advantages of using an MoE-specific masking i.e. MoE Expert Output Masking."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q471",
      "page": 55,
      "dimension": "input_ontology",
      "text": "Conditional MoE Routing (CMR). Instead of randomly dropping a proportion of activations or masking expert outputs, in this section, we consider the option of letting the model decide, and learn, which tokens need the extra capacity or specialization of MoE layers, and which tokens are better routed to a limited-capacity shared layer."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q472",
      "page": 55,
      "dimension": "input_ontology",
      "text": "Inspired by Zhang et al. (2021)'s CLSR-Gate, we design Conditional MoE Routing layers (CMR for short). As depicted in Figure 19, we augment MoE layers with a binary gate that decides the weights associated with two branches of the computational graph: (1) a shared dense FFN sublayer (FFNshared) and (2) an MoE layer with its own E expert FFN sublayers."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q473",
      "page": 55,
      "dimension": "input_ontology",
      "text": "Unlike Zhang et al. (2021)'s CLSR-Gate, our CMR branches are FFN sublayers (dense or sparsely gated MoE) and not linear projections. Furthermore, our CMR does not have language-specfic parameters, but learned routing to experts using an MoE layer."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q474",
      "page": 55,
      "dimension": "output_form",
      "text": "The CMR gate weights are learned by optimizing translation accuracy under a budget constraint p."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q475",
      "page": 56,
      "dimension": "input_ontology",
      "text": "Our baseline is a Sparsely Gated MoE model with model dimension 1024, FFN dimension 8192, 16 attention heads and 24 layers."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q476",
      "page": 56,
      "dimension": "input_ontology",
      "text": "We have 64 experts per MoE layer and we place an MoE layer in every alternate Transformer layer of the model (fMoE=2)."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q477",
      "page": 56,
      "dimension": "input_ontology",
      "text": "We compare this unregularized baseline to a variant with an overall dropout rate of 0.3 (pdrop=0.3), best performing after a sweep of pdrop ∈ {0.1, 0.2, 0.3}."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q478",
      "page": 56,
      "dimension": "output_form",
      "text": "For EOM, we sweep over the values of (pdrop, peom) ∈ {0.1, 0.2, 0.3}2 and choose the best out of 9 variants based on the average chrF++ score on the validation set."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q479",
      "page": 56,
      "dimension": "output_form",
      "text": "For FOM, we set pdrop=0.3 and sweep over pfom ∈ {0.1, 0.2, 0.3} and choose the best out of the variants based on the average chrF++ score on the validation set."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q480",
      "page": 56,
      "dimension": "input_ontology",
      "text": "For CMR, we train the baseline augmented with a shared FFN sublayer with the same dimensions as the rest of the model."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q481",
      "page": 56,
      "dimension": "output_form",
      "text": "We sweep over the values of (pdrop, pcmr) ∈ {0.1, 0.2, 0.3}2 and choose the best out of 9 variants based on the average chrF++ score on the validation set."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q482",
      "page": 56,
      "dimension": "output_form",
      "text": "Initial experiments on other benchmarks show that the value of p = 0.8 achieves the desirable trade-off of improving the performance on low-resource pairs without hindering the performance on high-resource ones."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q483",
      "page": 56,
      "dimension": "output_form",
      "text": "From our initial experiments, we find that the addition of the auxiliary budget constraint LCMR and pcmr are important for improving accuracy."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q484",
      "page": 57,
      "dimension": "output_form",
      "text": "For each model, we report chrF++ averages on the validation set in 3 groups of directions: eng_Latn-xx, xx-eng_Latn and xx-yy, broken down w.r.t. to resource levels: high, low and very low (v.low) for eng_Latn-xx and xx-eng_Latn."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q485",
      "page": 57,
      "dimension": "output_form",
      "text": "In terms of alleviating the overfitting issue, the last column of Figure 17 shows that EOM leads to better regularization and less overfitting on low-resource tasks compared to overall dropout."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q486",
      "page": 57,
      "dimension": "output_form",
      "text": "In terms of translation quality, and as shown in Table 16, we observe gains of +0.4 chrF++ across all pairs into English and +0.6 chrF++ across non-English pairs for MoE EOM compared to vanilla MoE with overall dropout."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q487",
      "page": 57,
      "dimension": "output_form",
      "text": "Gains are larger on low and very low-resource languages — for out of English, there are improvements of +0.6 and 0.9 chrF++ with EOM."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q488",
      "page": 57,
      "dimension": "input_ontology",
      "text": "The comparison between EOM and FOM proves that masking before combining the expert outputs is more beneficial than simply masking tokens in the final output."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q489",
      "page": 57,
      "dimension": "output_form",
      "text": "Our hypothesis is that this gain in performance stems from EOM strengthening the residual connection surrounding the MoE layer and reducing co-adaptation between selected top-2 experts, as well as co-adaptation between experts and the subsequent layers of the model."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q490",
      "page": 57,
      "dimension": "output_form",
      "text": "For CMR, we see +0.8 chrF++ across all pairs into English and +0.7 chrF++ across non-English pairs."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q491",
      "page": 57,
      "dimension": "output_form",
      "text": "Similarly, the improvements are larger for low and very low-resource languages, with +0.7 and +1.0 chrF++ respectively."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q492",
      "page": 57,
      "dimension": "output_form",
      "text": "CMR is computationally more expensive by 18-25% at training time because of the additional shared FFN layer at the level of each MoE layer in the model."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q493",
      "page": 57,
      "dimension": "output_form",
      "text": "Given the additional computational overhead, we use the simpler MoE EOM strategy."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q494",
      "page": 57,
      "dimension": "output_form",
      "text": "For Gating Dropout (Liu et al., 2022), we sweep over the values of (pdrop, pgd) ∈ {0.1, 0.2, 0.3}2 and choose the best out of 9 variants based on the average chrF++ score on the validation set."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q495",
      "page": 58,
      "dimension": "input_ontology",
      "text": "To reduce overfitting on low-resource language pairs further, we next explore alternative means of adding additional regularization. We try a straightforward curriculum of introducing these low-resource language pairs in phases during model training. The language pairs that empirically overfit within K updates are introduced K updates before the end of training."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q496",
      "page": 58,
      "dimension": "input_ontology",
      "text": "We train MoE-64 models with fMoE=2 for a total of T updates (see Section 6.2.1 for details of the base architecture). To derive the phases of the curriculum, we first train a regular model, i.e., without curriculum, then we partition language pairs into n buckets {b0, b1, . . . , bn−1} based on when they start to overfit."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q497",
      "page": 58,
      "dimension": "input_ontology",
      "text": "Based on observed overfitting patterns, we introduce pairs during training in n = 3 phases - we set T = 100k, k0 = 100k, k1 = 40k, k2 = 20k, so b0 is introduced first, b1 is introduced at step T − 40k, and b2 is introduced at step T − 20k."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q498",
      "page": 58,
      "dimension": "input_ontology",
      "text": "We compare to the baseline of an MoE model with overall dropout 0.3 without curriculum learning, i.e. introducing all pairs at the start of training and training for 100k updates."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q499",
      "page": 58,
      "dimension": "output_form",
      "text": "As shown in Table 17, for vanilla MoE, when translating out of English (eng_Latn-xx), there is an average improvement of +0.6 chrF++ on low-resource directions (low) and a +0.8 chrF++ improvement on very low-resource (v.low) directions."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q500",
      "page": 58,
      "dimension": "output_form",
      "text": "There is, however, no significant improvement on high-resource directions (high) or translation into English (xx-eng_Latn), most likely because there is no overfitting on these directions in the baseline."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q501",
      "page": 58,
      "dimension": "output_form",
      "text": "For MoE EOM, training with a curriculum actually hurts performance across eng_Latn-xx, xx-eng_Latn and xx-yy."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q502",
      "page": 58,
      "dimension": "output_form",
      "text": "Our analysis indicates that overfitting on the ablation dataset is already reduced by EOM, which has a higher fraction of language pairs with their best checkpoint by validation perplexity at ≥ 70000 steps."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q503",
      "page": 58,
      "dimension": "output_form",
      "text": "We hypothesize that adding a curriculum on top of EOM is not needed for the ablation dataset."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q504",
      "page": 58,
      "dimension": "output_form",
      "text": "However, results in Table 29 show that with the full dataset and larger model, combining curriculum learning and EOM improves performance, especially on low and very low-resource language pairs."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q505",
      "page": 58,
      "dimension": "input_ontology",
      "text": "MoE theoretically enables models to specialize expert capacity for different tasks, but what do these models actually learn?"
    },
    {
      "id": "Q506",
      "page": 58,
      "dimension": "input_form",
      "text": "We now take a closer look at the routing of tokens to experts in MoE layers at different points of the encoder-decoder architecture. We take an MoE model (E=64, pdrop=0.3, peom=0.2) trained on our ablation dataset and do a forward pass on Flores-200 dev set data in teacher-forcing mode, i.e., we feed the true target prefix to predict the next target token."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q507",
      "page": 58,
      "dimension": "output_form",
      "text": "For each task (language pair), we log the routing decisions prior to Top-k-Gating, and depending on whether it is an encoder layer or a decoder layer, we average the routing vectors across multiple language pairs to estimate language-level routing vectors."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q508",
      "page": 59,
      "dimension": "output_form",
      "text": "Table 17: Curriculum Learning Results demonstrate that for vanilla MoE, training on a curriculum reduces overfitting, particularly for eng_Latn-xx low and very low resource pairs. For MoE EOM, a curriculum does not help."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q509",
      "page": 59,
      "dimension": "input_form",
      "text": "where T<lang> is the set of all tokens in <lang>, source-side for encoder layers and target-side for decoder layers."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q510",
      "page": 59,
      "dimension": "output_form",
      "text": "The similarity heatmaps demonstrate that in late decoder layers (see Figure 20d), the languages are being separated, i.e., dispatched to different set of experts."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q511",
      "page": 59,
      "dimension": "output_form",
      "text": "Languages within the same family are highly similar in their choice of experts, i.e., the late decoder MoE layers are language-specific."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q512",
      "page": 59,
      "dimension": "output_form",
      "text": "This is particularly the case for languages in the Atlantic-Congo family (the rows/columns from cjk to yor) and some pairs like {snd_Arab, urd_Arab} in the Indo-European family or {yue_Hant, zho_Hans} in the Sino-Tibetan family."
    },
    {
      "id": "Q513",
